profiles.name: Asian Elephant
profiles.intro: An elephant’s journeys help shape forests. Protecting connected habitat helps people and elephants share space.
profiles.habitat: Forests and adjoining landscapes across South and Southeast Asia.
profiles.threats: Habitat loss and fragmentation, conflict with people, poaching, and illegal capture.
profiles.protection: Restore habitat corridors, reduce conflict around farms, and prevent illegal wildlife trade.
profiles.fact: Elephants spread seeds as they move through the forest.

conservation.note: This category refers to the Asian elephant species, not a particular national population.

profiles.name: West African Lion
profiles.intro: The lion’s story changes with geography. West Africa’s remaining lions need protection even though the species has a different global category.
profiles.habitat: Savannas and woodland landscapes in West Africa, including Senegal’s Niokolo-Koba National Park.
profiles.threats: Shrinking habitat, loss of wild prey, poaching, snares, and conflict over livestock.
profiles.protection: Support protected-area patrols, monitor populations, safeguard prey, and improve coexistence with communities.
profiles.fact: Lions live in social groups called prides.

conservation.note: The regional West African status must not be presented as the category for every lion worldwide.

profiles.name: Malayan Tiger
profiles.intro: A forest predator and a symbol of Malaysia. Protecting the Malayan tiger means tackling poaching while keeping forests connected and prey secure.
profiles.threats: Poaching and illegal trade, forest loss and fragmentation, and overhunting of prey.
profiles.protection: Anti-poaching patrols, wildlife monitoring, habitat protection, and public conservation education.
profiles.fact: Panthera tigris jacksoni is used in the traditional subspecies classification; tiger taxonomy is under review.

conservation.note: WWF-Malaysia reports the Malayan tiger as Critically Endangered. This differs from the global species category; subspecies taxonomy is under review.

profiles.name: Indochinese Leopard
profiles.intro: A leopard can vanish quietly from a forest. The Indochinese subspecies faces exceptional pressure, making its remaining strongholds especially important.
profiles.habitat: Southeast Asian forests; important remaining strongholds include Peninsular Malaysia and the Thailand–Myanmar border region.
profiles.threats: Poaching, snaring, illegal trade, loss of habitat and prey, and conflict with people.
profiles.protection: Strengthen anti-poaching work, protect remaining forest strongholds, and monitor leopards and their prey.
profiles.fact: Many Indochinese leopards in the Malay Peninsula have a dark, melanistic coat.

conservation.note: The subspecies category is more severe than the global category for Panthera pardus.

profiles.name: Formosan Black Bear
profiles.intro: Taiwan’s native bear lives in mountain forests. Its local conservation needs deserve their own story alongside the status of the Asiatic black bear species.
profiles.habitat: Broadleaf, mixed, and coniferous mountain forests in Taiwan.
profiles.threats: Habitat deterioration and fragmentation, road development, illegal hunting, and accidental trapping.
profiles.protection: Safeguard connected forest habitat, reduce accidental trapping, and support community conservation and monitoring.
profiles.fact: The Formosan black bear is an endemic Taiwanese subspecies of the Asiatic black bear.

conservation.note: The game’s Vulnerable label reflects the global species category. Taiwan lists the Formosan population as Nationally Endangered in 2024, a separate assessment.

profiles.name: African Wild Dog
profiles.intro: Life in a pack depends on room to roam. African wild dogs need connected landscapes to hunt, raise pups, and move between territories.
profiles.habitat: Grasslands, woodlands, and other habitats, with major populations in southern and eastern Africa.
profiles.threats: Habitat fragmentation, conflict with people, accidental and deliberate killing, and infectious disease.
profiles.protection: Maintain wildlife corridors, reduce livestock conflict, and support community conservation and population monitoring.
profiles.fact: Each wild dog has its own distinctive pattern of coloured patches.

conservation.note: The status shown here applies to Lycaon pictus worldwide.

profiles.name: Leopard Cat
profiles.intro: A small wild cat with a wide range. Least Concern globally does not mean safe everywhere: local populations can still need urgent protection.
profiles.habitat: Forests, shrublands, and some farmed landscapes across mainland Asia, including Taiwan.
profiles.threats: Local habitat loss, hunting and trade, snares, retaliation over poultry, and road mortality.
profiles.protection: Protect habitat refuges, reduce snaring and wildlife trade, and address road and community conflict risks.
profiles.fact: Leopard cats hunt small prey, especially rodents, and can climb and swim.

conservation.note: The game does not specify a local population. The Taiwan assessment is additional context, not an assumed identity for the piece.

profiles.name: Aquatic Rat
profiles.intro: The game’s Aquatic Rat label and UK conservation note appear to refer to a water vole. This identification needs confirmation from the designer.
profiles.habitat: For water voles: vegetated banks of rivers, streams, ditches, ponds, and wetlands.
profiles.threats: For water voles: habitat loss and degradation, pollution, and predation by introduced American mink.
profiles.protection: Restore connected riverbank habitat, monitor populations, and support coordinated mink management by conservation groups.
profiles.fact: Water voles have a rounded nose, small ears, and a furry tail.

conservation.scope: Water vole · Great Britain Red List

profiles.name: Tree Pangolin
profiles.intro: A small forest mammal with a remarkable climbing tail. The tree pangolin is also known as the white-bellied pangolin.
profiles.habitat: Forests of western and central Africa, where it climbs trees and also forages on the ground.
profiles.threats: Hunting for meat and scales, illegal wildlife trade, and loss of forest habitat.
profiles.protection: Protect forests, reduce illegal trade, and support local monitoring and conservation work.
profiles.fact: Its prehensile tail helps it grip branches while climbing.

conservation.note: This story uses the white-bellied pangolin identity associated with the name Tree Pangolin.

profiles.name: Iberian Lynx
profiles.intro: A conservation recovery still in progress. The Iberian lynx has returned to more places, but its future depends on continued protection.
profiles.habitat: Mediterranean scrub and woodland mosaics in Spain and Portugal.
profiles.threats: Loss of rabbit prey, fragmented habitat, road collisions, and illegal killing.
profiles.protection: Restore rabbit populations and habitat, maintain safe connections, and continue monitoring and recovery programmes.
profiles.fact: European rabbits are its main prey; rabbit disease can therefore threaten lynx recovery.

conservation.note: Assessed as Vulnerable in 2024. Recovery does not mean conservation work can stop.

sources.name: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group · Iberian lynx

profiles.name: Philippine Eagle
profiles.intro: A forest guardian found only in the Philippines. Protecting this eagle also protects the forest communities around it.
profiles.threats: Forest loss and hunting reduce the safe places where eagles can live and breed.
profiles.protection: Protect nesting forests, support forest guards and local communities, and maintain rescue and conservation breeding programmes.
profiles.fact: The Philippine eagle is the national bird of the Philippines.

conservation.note: The conservation category applies to the Philippine eagle species.

sources.name: Philippine Eagle Foundation · The Philippine eagle
sources.supports: Species identity, ecology, conservation context and protection

profiles.name: Green Sea Turtle
profiles.intro: A long ocean journey connects feeding grounds with nesting beaches. Global recovery is encouraging, while local turtle populations still need care.
profiles.habitat: Tropical and subtropical seas, including coastal feeding grounds and sandy nesting beaches.
profiles.threats: Accidental capture in fishing gear, loss of nesting habitat, direct take, pollution, and climate change.
profiles.protection: Reduce fishing bycatch, protect nesting beaches and coastal habitat, and support monitoring and responsible coastal use.
profiles.fact: Adult green turtles feed mainly on seagrasses and algae.

conservation.note: Global IUCN category updated in 2025. Regional populations can remain threatened; US legal listings use separate population assessments.

profiles.name: Grévy's Zebra
profiles.intro: Fine stripes and large ears distinguish this endangered zebra. Sharing grasslands and water safely is central to its future.
profiles.habitat: Dry grasslands and savannas in Kenya and Ethiopia.
profiles.threats: Habitat loss, competition for grazing and water, drought, hunting, and disease.
profiles.protection: Support community conservation, protect access to water and grazing, and monitor populations.
profiles.fact: Each zebra has its own distinctive stripe pattern.

conservation.note: The category describes Grevy’s zebra, rather than all zebra species.

profiles.name: Blue Whale
profiles.intro: The largest animal on Earth feeds on tiny prey. Blue whales are recovering from historic whaling, but human activity still brings risks.
profiles.habitat: Oceans worldwide, moving between feeding and breeding areas.
profiles.threats: Vessel strikes and entanglement in fishing gear, with additional risks from ocean noise and changing habitat.
profiles.protection: Reduce vessel collisions and entanglement, protect important habitat, and monitor whale populations.
profiles.fact: Blue whales filter small crustaceans called krill through baleen plates.

conservation.scope: US Endangered Species Act · species listing
conservation.note: The category shown is the US Endangered Species Act listing reported by NOAA; it is not presented as a newly verified global IUCN assessment.
